title: Per-tick worker sandboxes: one container per tick
description:
The Phase 2 headline. Phase 1 boots ONE orchestrator sandbox that runs the skill loop with harness-native subagents inside it; Phase 2 gives every tick its own container.

Per the design: clone at the epic base, branch tick/<epic-id>/<tick-id>, implement, push branch plus RESULT-<tick-id>.md, exit. Collect reads ONLY what survived in git — commits, the result file, the .tick/ boundary diff — never sandbox terminal output.

All three spawn-time defences the herd substrate documents apply verbatim here and must be implemented, not assumed:
- the GREEN-START TRAP: a cleanly started container that did nothing. Probe with trivial work before dispatching real work. Phase 1 already proved this class twice (an npx probe returning npm version; a Codex self-update swallowing the gate).
- CONFIRMED DISPATCH: wait for evidence of work starting, not just process start.
- EXPIRING LIVENESS: re-check aliveness immediately before any destructive action.

Cost note this tick must respect: a container per tick means the image cold-start cost is paid N times per wave. Coordinate with kuf — its numbers decide whether sleeping named sandboxes amortise the pull well enough for this to be affordable at width 5.
notes:
2026-08-21 13:50 - Measured argument FOR this tick, from Phase 1 runs. The Phase 1 sandbox is instance_type standard-3: 2 vCPU, 8 GiB memory, 16 GB disk, with max_instances = 3. Run 62c289d1 put SEVEN implementer subagents in that one container; run a1f87597 put one. Per-implementer throughput was 0.78 calls/min with seven and 2.71 with one — about 3.5x slower each. The comparison is confounded (different ticks, different work), so treat it as direction rather than a coefficient, but 7 concurrent implementers running greps, go builds and pnpm installs on 2 vCPU is exactly the contention this tick removes.

Disk is the sharper limit: the comment on instance_type already says the batteries-included image is multi-GB before a checkout, and run 62c289d1 created seven worktrees of this repo in one 16 GB container, each accumulating build output and module caches.

Two things this tick must not skip: max_instances = 3 is a deployment ceiling, so a wave wider than 3 needs it raised (bounded by the account's container limits) or the wave will silently serialise; and kuf must measure whether N image pulls per wave are amortised by sleeping named sandboxes, because per-tick containers pay cold start N times.
2026-08-21 18:09 - kuf's numbers, which this tick was waiting on (2026-08-21, linux/amd64, image digest sha256:bba89942..., measured off-platform with docker — treat as shape, not as Cloudflare absolutes):

COST IS NOT THE OBJECTION. Cold start is $0.0042 per run on standard-3; a fully cold wave of SIX containers costs 2.5 cents. Against $4-6 of model spend per epic that is noise, so 'a container per tick pays cold start N times' is answered: pay it. The cost note in this tick's description can be closed out as measured.

TIME IS THE OBJECTION, AND IT IS NOT THE IMAGE PULL. Cold 93.2s, of which image pull is 71.9s, clone 3.3s, toolchain 0.7s, deps 17.0s, container start 0.4s. But fan-out per-sandbox degrades 1.00x/2.22x/3.74x at N=1/3/5 and kuf reports ALL of that degradation is in dependency install, not the pull. So the thing to design around is concurrent dependency installs, not registry bandwidth.

Also settled by wave 3: x3v found that on Cloudflare an image belongs to the [[containers]] application, not to a boot — getSandbox has no image parameter — so per-tick containers all run the SAME image and a per-repo image is a deployment-time choice. And max_instances = 3 is a deployment ceiling that will silently serialise a wave wider than 3; raising it is bounded by the account's container limits.

Read docs/sandbox-start-benchmark.md before designing; it answers three decisions with a number each.

2026-08-21 19:42 - Scope answered: yes, file them — the worker's container-side entrypoint (kx8) and the wiring that calls dispatchWave (7wq) are now separate ticks, and bmo/s7f/bne stay blocked until at least kx8 lands. Splitting here was the right call rather than one enormous tick: the dispatch layer is independently testable and now is, at 39 tests, and the entrypoint is a different substrate (a container's own program, closer to cloud/sandbox/entrypoint.sh than to the Worker).
acceptance_criteria: A wave of N ticks runs in N containers concurrently; each pushes its branch and RESULT file and collect reads only the durable layer; a container that starts cleanly but does no work is caught by the probe rather than counted as launched; a killed container is detected before any destructive action.
closed_reason: Completed for the mechanism it owns: a dispatch layer that boots one sandbox per tick, fans N out concurrently, and implements all three spawn-time defences as behaviour rather than assumption — a probe checked for its expected marker rather than its exit code, a dispatch confirmed by observed work rather than by process start, and a liveness check taken immediately before anything destructive. Collect reads only the durable git layer. The container-side worker entrypoint and the call site are filed as kx8 and 7wq.
